doc.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The Venezuelan youth orchestra and its young conductor
summary: Jones and Baker praise the Venezuelan youth orchestra and its young conductor, who has taken 500,000 former street kids and taught them instruments; Jones says they will receive the Q prize.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Oh yes. The guy’s got all those kids.
Him and his mentor. He’s taking over from Esa-Pekka [Salonen]. You know that?

I heard that orchestra when they did the Bartok concerto for orchestra, before they got into the Latin – it’s the most amazing thing I’ve heard, and it’s been perpetuated. The guy who – the older guy . . .
We give them – both of them, as mentor. It’s about mentors. The mentor and him. He’s 27 years old.
A monster. He’s taking over the L.A. Philharmonic from Esa-Pekka. You know that?
He is. He’s going to be the permanent conductor of the L.A. Philharmonic. It’s awesome. We’ll give him the Q prize in the next two months.

What he did – because when – I was not in the room when they started, and I said, is that the Chicago? that brass? I walk in, and instead of it being four people at the bass trombone, it was about six or seven of them. And when they got done, then they had a kind of fun time. They were playing – the clavé was going so heavy, you couldn’t stop moving. This cat has done this, and it’s perpetuating.

The good parts about it, the kids have got cuts – throat’s cut and gun wounds and everything. They’re ex-street gangsters. That’s what they come from. That’s what I mean made me cry. It’s he’s taken 500,000 of these little suckers and turned them around. Got them playing violin and flutes and woodwinds and stuff. Wow.
Everything. It’s unbelievable. I see these faces, knife cuts all over them. Unbelievable. Anyway, the dots are getting connected.
